title: All companions gone
hook: every companion left, none stayed to the end; only the Lord remains (Salok M9 55, ang 1429)

segments.voice: Yesterday: strength returned, and your line: all is in your hands. Did you send a few words to someone stuck? Today, a salok about who is still there when the hard part comes. Day six hundred six.
screen: `STRENGTH RETURNED — ALL IS IN YOUR HANDS.`

segments.voice: Hospital waiting rooms tell the truth about friendship. At the wedding there were two hundred people. At the birthday, the house was full. Then someone gets a long illness, and by the third month the visitors thin out. Nobody means it. People get busy; they don't know what to say; they assume someone else is going. And the patient notices, quietly, who is still coming on Tuesday afternoons. Guru Tegh Bahadur has a two-line salok about that thinning out. It's a stark line. And the story around it holds a surprise. Today: all companions gone.
screen: `TWO HUNDRED AT THE WEDDING.` → `THE VISITORS THIN OUT.` → `WHO STILL COMES ON TUESDAY.`

segments.voice: Salok fifty-five, Ang fourteen twenty-nine. In paraphrase: all my companions and friends have left me; no one kept company with me to the end. Nanak says, in this calamity, my one support is the Lord. Sang sakhaa: companions, friends. Sabh taj gae: all have abandoned, all have gone. Kou na nibhio saath: no one saw the companionship through. Nibhaana is a rich Punjabi verb. It means to keep something going to the end: to keep a promise, to keep a friendship, to keep faith when it costs. Then the second line: in this bipat, this disaster, the one tek, the one prop, is the Lord. The salok uses the name Raghunaath, a name for God that Gurbani borrows from the old stories of Rama. This continues the run of saloks we've been reading: Rama gone, nothing stays, strength gone. Now the people go too, and what remains is God. Here is the surprise. Sikh tradition remembers that when Guru Tegh Bahadur was held in Delhi, three Sikhs did stay with him: Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das, and Bhai Dayala. Tradition says they were executed in front of him, before his own death, and Sikhs remember them by name to this day. So the salok describes the way of the world, and the story honors the rare people who refused to be the way of the world. That's the double edge of the line. It names where the salok finds the final support. And it quietly asks: when someone you love is in the bipat, will you be the one who nibhaaes, who sees it through?
screen: `SANG SAKHAA: ALL MY COMPANIONS LEFT.` · `NIBHAANA: SEEING IT THROUGH.` · `THE ONE PROP IN THE DISASTER.` · `THREE WHO STAYED IN DELHI.` · then, large: `HE REMAINS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be one who stays. Sit, and remember a time someone stayed with you through something hard: who kept calling, who kept showing up. Thank them silently. Then think of someone in a long hard stretch now, an illness, a grief, a lonely year, whose visitors may have thinned out. Picture yourself as the Tuesday afternoon visitor, not the crowd at the wedding. What would staying look like this week? A call, a meal dropped off, ten minutes sitting with them. Choose one. If you pray, you can hold them before God and say Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Tek, a prop, a support. Sang sakhaa sabh taj gae: everyone left, and in the bipat, the one tek is the Lord.
Your line: he remains. Do the one staying thing you chose, today if you can, for someone in a long hard stretch. Day six hundred six.

howItsDone: Salok fifty-five is read among the closing saloks of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs remember Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das and Bhai Dayala, who stayed with Guru Tegh Bahadur in Delhi.

fork.setup: a friend's long illness is in its third month and the visitors have thinned out. you're busy too. what does the story around salok fifty-five honor?
options: sending a card and moving on.
being the one who stays to the end.
fork.reveal: the salok names the world's way, and Sikhs honor the three who refused it and stayed with the Guru in Delhi.

original.note: Gurmukhi: tek, a prop or support; salok fifty-five calls the Lord the one tek in the calamity.

trapdoor: what you thought: all companions gone is a complaint about friends.
what it means: people go, the Lord remains; and the rare friend who stays is honored.
what a scholar hears: the line hinges on nibhio saath, seeing companionship through; tradition places Bhai Mati Das, Sati Das and Dayala with the Guru at his martyrdom.

sources.ref: Salok Mahalla 9, salok 55 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429)

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the superlative 'one of the starkest lines in his bani' and the 1675 date; the narrator no longer tells the listener where the final support lies; the practice now starts from someone who stayed with the listener, so it doesn't repeat day 605's picture-someone-stuck practice.
Transliteration sang sakhaa sabh taj gae kou na nibhio saath / kahu naanak ih bipat mai tek ek raghunaath: confirm.
The three are not named individually in the standard Ardas (they fall under its martyrs lines); the script says only that Sikhs remember them by name.
Order of executions (the three before the Guru): traditional; confirm.
